title: Privacy strings and permissions: camera, location, photos and tracking

videos.script: An app cannot open the camera until the person holding the phone says yes. {{alert}} And it is iOS that asks, not the app. The app supplies one sentence, and the system puts it in an alert it draws itself. It asks once. A person who says no is never asked again. {{table}} So this lesson is about asking for as little as possible. The planner gets one new feature, a photo of your notes, and one key to go with it. {{picker}} Choosing an existing photo needs no permission at all, because the system's picker runs outside the app. {{location}} Location and tracking get a look too, and the planner needs neither. {{manifest}} Then the privacy manifest, the file that declares what the app does without asking. You write a small checker that reads both files on Linux, {{missing}} and watch it catch the key that would have crashed the app. {{denied}} Last, the answer no. The planner keeps working, and the camera button becomes a sentence and a way to Settings.
